```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

`mglpa` implements, entirely in R, the sequence of multi-group tests of
profile similarity proposed by Morin, Meyer, Creusier and Biétry (2016) for
latent profile analysis (LPA) with continuous indicators:

0. **Class enumeration** in each group (how many profiles?);
1. **Configural similarity** (same number of profiles in every group);
2. **Structural similarity** (same profile means);
3. **Dispersion similarity** (same within-profile variances);
4. **Distributional similarity** (same profile proportions);
5. **Predictive similarity** (same relations between predictors and profile
   membership);
6. **Explanatory similarity** (same profile-specific levels of distal outcomes).

The models are diagonal Gaussian mixtures estimated by maximum likelihood with
an EM algorithm and Mplus-style random starts. The package reproduces the
log-likelihoods, free-parameter counts, information criteria and entropy that
Mplus reports for the same models (the conventions are described at the end).

The random starts in this vignette are kept small so that it builds quickly;
use many more in practice (for example `starts = c(500, 50)` or more). The EM
iterations of the enumeration and similarity models run in compiled C++ code,
and `cores = n` distributes the random starts over several CPU cores.

## Data

The example data set contains five standardized working-memory indicators for
500 younger and 500 older adults, two predictors and two distal outcomes.

```{r}
library(mglpa)
data(mglpa_wm)
head(mglpa_wm)
ind <- c("verbal_wm", "visual_wm", "updating", "inhibition", "proc_speed")
```

## Step 0: class enumeration

```{r}
enum <- enumerate_profiles(mglpa_wm, ind, group = "group", k = 1:4,
                           starts = c(20, 4), seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
enum
elbow_plot(enum)
```

The columns `VLMR_p` and `aLMR_p` are the p-values of the Vuong-Lo-Mendell-Rubin
likelihood ratio test and of its adjusted version, which compare each solution
with the solution with one profile less (the Mplus `TECH11` output; see
`vlmr_test()`). The bootstrap likelihood ratio test (`TECH14`) is added with
`enumeration_blrt()`; very few draws are used here to keep the vignette fast:

```{r}
enum <- enumeration_blrt(enum, B = 10, starts = c(5, 2), seed = 11, verbose = FALSE)
enumeration_table(enum)[, c("group", "k", "LRT", "VLMR_p", "aLMR_p", "BLRT_p")]
```

The classification quality of a solution (entropy and the average posterior
probabilities of the observations assigned to each profile, the tables printed
by Mplus) is obtained with `classification_quality()`:

```{r}
classification_quality(enum$fits[["1"]][["3"]])
```

The three-profile solution has the lowest BIC and CAIC in both groups. Its
profiles can be inspected with `profile_plot()` (z scores computed with the
sample mean and standard deviation of each indicator):

```{r}
profile_plot(enum$fits[["1"]][["3"]], title = "Younger adults, 3 profiles")
```

## Steps 1 to 4: similarity tests

```{r}
sim <- similarity_tests(mglpa_wm, ind, group = "group", k = 3,
                        starts = c(30, 5), seed = 2, verbose = FALSE)
sim
```

Each model is compared with the previous one. Similarity is supported when at
least two of CAIC, BIC and ABIC decrease. Here structural and dispersion
similarity are supported and distributional similarity is rejected: the
profiles have the same shape and the same within-profile variability in both
groups, but their sizes differ.

```{r}
profile_proportions(sim$fits$dispersion)
profile_plot(sim$fits$dispersion, type = "line", title = "Dispersion similarity model")
```

APA-style tables can be produced and written to a Word-compatible file:

```{r}
apa_table(sim)
# write_table_doc(apa_table(sim), "similarity.doc", title = "Table 2")
```

## Step 5: predictive similarity

The profile solution is held fixed at the estimates of the most constrained
model supported (the dispersion model), and profile membership is regressed on
the predictors with group-specific or equal effects.

```{r}
pred <- predictive_similarity(sim, predictors = c("education", "cog_reserve"),
                              seed = 3, verbose = FALSE)
pred
```

## Step 6: explanatory similarity

Distal outcomes are added as indicators whose means may differ across
profiles and groups; the profile solution is again held fixed.

```{r}
expl <- explanatory_similarity(sim, outcomes = c("task_perf", "everyday_func"),
                               outcome_variances = "equal", seed = 4, verbose = FALSE)
expl
head(expl$contrasts$free_means_equal_var)
```

## Fitting a single model

Every model of the sequence can be specified directly:

```{r}
m <- mglpa_model(3, ind, group = "group", equal_means = TRUE)
fit <- fit_lpa(mglpa_wm, m, starts = c(20, 4), seed = 5)
fit
head(parameters(fit))
```

`reorder_profiles()` relabels the profiles (by level, by size, or with an
explicit permutation); `fixed_from_fit()` extracts estimates to hold them
fixed in a later model; `contrast_estimates()` computes any linear combination
of parameters with delta-method standard errors.

## The Shiny application

`mglpa_app()` opens a graphical interface with the same workflow: data import,
enumeration, similarity tests, profile plots, predictive and explanatory
similarity, tables and project files.

## Conventions shared with Mplus

* `ESTIMATOR = MLR`: standard errors are sandwich estimates based on the
  observed information matrix (`se = "robust"`).
* For `KNOWNCLASS` models Mplus includes the known-group proportions in the
  log-likelihood and counts them as free parameters, and (up to version 8)
  computes entropy over the latent class patterns (profiles x groups).
  `fit_lpa()` follows these conventions when `mplus_convention = TRUE` (the
  default), so that the values are directly comparable with Mplus output.
  Mplus 9 instead reports a profile-specific entropy ("Classification
  Quality for C"), which corresponds to `fit$entropy_profiles`.
* When predictors of profile membership are brought into the model, Mplus
  treats them as multivariate normal variables; their saturated means,
  variances and covariances are added to the log-likelihood and to the
  parameter count. Regression coefficients and all model comparisons are
  unaffected.
* Predictive and explanatory models hold the profile solution fixed at the
  values of the retained similarity model rounded to five decimals, like
  Mplus start values (`digits = 5`).
* `TECH11`: the Vuong-Lo-Mendell-Rubin test uses the weight matrix of Vuong
  (1989) with the robust (sandwich) covariance matrices of the two models in
  place of their inverse information matrices, as Mplus does (Vermunt, 2024),
  p-values computed with Imhof's method, and the adjustment of Lo, Mendell and
  Rubin (2001), which divides the statistic by 1 + 1 / (d log N). `vlmr_test()`
  reproduces the statistic, mean, standard deviation and p-values of the Mplus
  output; `variant = "vuong"` gives Vuong's original matrix (the implementation
  of LatentGOLD).
* `TECH14`: the bootstrap p-value is the proportion of bootstrap statistics at
  least as large as the observed one; in every generated data set the
  (k - 1)-profile model is started from the parent estimates and the k-profile
  model uses random starts (`LRTSTARTS`). Mplus chooses the number of draws
  adaptively, `blrt()` uses the fixed number `B`. Like Mplus, `blrt()` warns
  when draws with a statistic below the observed one did not replicate their
  best log-likelihood or did not converge (possible local maxima that
  understate the bootstrap statistic) and reports the largest p-value they
  could produce (`p_upper`); draws above the observed statistic whose
  (k - 1)-profile model did not converge may overstate it, and `p_lower` is
  the smallest p-value they could produce. Non-converged draws are always
  listed in the warnings.
* Classification quality: the same two tables as Mplus (average posterior
  probabilities by most likely profile, and probabilities of the most likely
  profile given the profile); for `KNOWNCLASS` models they are computed within
  each known group.

## References

Lo, Y., Mendell, N. R., & Rubin, D. B. (2001). Testing the number of components
in a normal mixture. *Biometrika, 88*(3), 767-778.

Morin, A. J. S., Meyer, J. P., Creusier, J., & Biétry, F. (2016). Multiple-group
analysis of similarity in latent profile solutions. *Organizational Research
Methods, 19*(2), 231-254. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428115621148

Vermunt, J. K. (2024). The Vuong-Lo-Mendell-Rubin test for latent class and
latent profile analysis: A note on the different implementations in Mplus and
LatentGOLD. *Methodology, 20*(1), Article e12467.
https://doi.org/10.5964/meth.12467

Vuong, Q. H. (1989). Likelihood ratio tests for model selection and non-nested
hypotheses. *Econometrica, 57*(2), 307-333.
